title: Local vs Global Scope
objective: Understand where a variable is visible and why functions can't see each other's local variables.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Scope is drawn out as its own chapter from concepts embedded throughout the book's Functions chapter. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A variable created inside a function is local to that function — it exists only while the function is running, and no code outside that function can see it, not even other functions.

A variable created at the top level of your script, outside any function, is global — every function can read it. But a function can't change a global variable just by assigning to a name with the same word inside its body; that assignment creates a brand-new local variable instead, which quietly shadows the global one.

Each function call gets its own fresh set of local variables, even if you call the same function twice in a row. Nothing from one call carries over into the next unless it's passed in or read from a global.
explanation.rule: A variable created inside a function only exists inside that function; it disappears when the function finishes.

examples.title: A Local Variable Stays Local
examples.code:
def heat_metal():
    temperature = 1200
    print(temperature)

heat_metal()
# print(temperature)  # NameError: temperature only existed inside heat_metal()
examples.note: temperature is created and destroyed entirely within heat_metal(); nothing outside the function can see it.

checks.question: A variable is created inside function_a(). Can function_b() read it?
options: Yes, all functions share every variable.
No — a local variable only exists inside the function that created it.
Only if function_b() is defined first.
Only if the variable is named the same in both functions.

feedback.correct: Correct — local variables are private to the function that created them.
feedback.incorrect: Local variables don't leak out of the function they're created in, even to other functions.

assignment.title: Local Counter
assignment.brief: Write count_ingots() that creates a local variable count set to 5 and prints it, then call it twice in a row to show each call starts fresh.
requirements: Define count_ingots() with a local variable count = 5.
assignment.starterCode:
def count_ingots():
    # Create a local variable count = 5 and print it.
    pass

count_ingots()
count_ingots()
assignment.solutionCode:
def count_ingots():
    count = 5
    print(count)

count_ingots()
count_ingots()
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    count_ingots()
    count_ingots()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.outputCheckLabel: count_ingots() called twice prints 5 both times

hints: Create count = 5 inside the function body, then print(count).
Each call to count_ingots() creates a fresh local count — they don't affect each other.
Call the function twice, exactly as the starter code already sets up.
The output should be 5 on one line, then 5 again on the next.
